title: Paano Magtanim ng Abaka: How to Plant Abaca the Traditional Way
metaTitle: Paano Magtanim ng Abaka: The Traditional Way, Step by Step
metaDescription: Paano magtanim ng abaka? See how traditional farmers plant abaka step by step, with the days, the spacing and what to change for a higher yield.
excerpt: Paano magtanim ng abaka? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant abaka (abaca), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Banana plants with bagged bunches along a farm road in Panabo City

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant abaka. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino abaca farmers in Bicol, Eastern Visayas, Davao, Caraga and other uplands usually set up an abaca farm from suckers or corm pieces and care for it until the first stalks are stripped for fiber. It also shows where the usual small farm differs from a well kept one.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for banana and abaca](/land-preparation/banana-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [abaka varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/abaca). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [abaka nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/abaca-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing.
When to plant abaka

Plant as the rains begin so the young plants get steady water. Where rain falls well through the whole year, as on the Pacific side of Bicol, Samar and eastern Mindanao, planting can go on in any month. Clearing is best done in the dry months before.
What you plant

Most farmers dig suckers from healthy old mats: immature suckers about 9 to 11 months old and at least 1 m tall take best, while small sword suckers about half a meter tall die more often. Others plant corm pieces (seedpieces) with at least three good eyes, single eye pieces, or tissue culture plantlets bought from a nursery and hardened for about three months. Farmers trim the roots, clean off rotten parts, cut back the leaves and throw out any corm with weevil tunnels, and never take material from a mat with bunchy top or mosaic.
Paano magtanim ng abaka, step by step
The first stalks are cut at about 16 to 24 months. After that the same mat is harvested every 3 to 4 months for many years. The crop is ready about 20 months after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 2 months before planting: Clear the land and keep the shade
items.text: In the dry months, cut the shrubs and grass close to the ground and pile them to rot instead of burning. Keep or plant shade trees such as katuray, anii, dapdap, ipil ipil or coconut, since abaca wants about half shade. Tip: Under coconuts, the coconut trees should stand at least 10 m apart or the abaca gets too dark.

items.title: 30 days before planting: Plow where you can
items.text: Where a plow can get in, as on open land or under coconuts, plow deep one or two times so the soil turns loose and the mat of coconut roots is broken up. On steep land, just clear and dig.

items.title: 14 days before planting: Lay out and stake the hills
items.text: Run straight lines east to west and push a stick about 1 m long where each hill will go, usually in squares of 2.5 m by 2.5 m. Varieties that make few suckers go closer, at 1.5 m by 1.5 m.

items.title: 7 days before planting: Dig the holes
items.text: Dig a hole deep enough for the sucker or corm, putting the dark topsoil on one side and the paler subsoil on the other.

items.title: 2 days before planting: Dig and clean the planting material
items.text: Dig suckers or corms from healthy mats only. Trim the roots, cut away rotten parts and cut back the leaves so the plant loses less water. Tip: Leave out any mat with yellow streaks, bunched leaves or a shrunken top. Those carry virus.

parts.title: Go only to healthy mats
parts.text: Take planting material only from mats of strong, healthy mother plants in a farm free of virus. Walk the mats first and pass by any with yellow streaks, bunched leaves or a stunted top.

parts.title: Choose immature suckers
parts.text: The best suckers are immature ones about 9 to 11 months old and at least 1 m tall. Leave the small sword suckers of about half a meter, which die often after planting.

parts.title: Or cut corm pieces
parts.text: Where suckers are few, dig a healthy corm and cut it into seedpieces that each carry at least three good eyes, or into single eye pieces with one plump bud each.

parts.title: Trim and clean
parts.text: Cut off the old roots and every rotten or dark part, and cut back the leaves so the plant loses less water. Throw out any corm with weevil tunnels in it.

parts.title: Guard against corm weevil
parts.text: Where corm weevil is a problem, many farmers soak the seedpieces or suckers in an insecticide dip before planting.

parts.title: Keep your tools clean
parts.text: Wash and wipe the bolo, knife and spade between mats, since dirty tools carry disease from one hill to the next.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant and press the soil
items.text: Put a little fertilizer, with compost if you have it, in the bottom of the hole and cover it with some topsoil. Set the sucker or corm in, fill first with topsoil then with subsoil, and press the soil firm so water does not pool in the hole. Tip: Leave a stick beside every corm or eye piece so you can find it before it sprouts.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 21: Replace the missing hills
items.text: Visit the field two to three weeks after planting and plant again where nothing grew, using immature suckers from healthy mats.

items.title: Day 30: Ring weed every month or two
items.text: Clear the weeds in a ring around each young plant so you can see the hills, and leave the cut weeds to rot as mulch.

items.title: Month 2: First fertilizer
items.text: Between one and three months after planting, scatter fertilizer mixed with compost a little away from the base of each plant, on moist soil.

items.title: Month 3: Watch for virus and weevils
items.text: Walk the farm every month looking for bunchy top, mosaic and bract mosaic, and for aphids on the young leaves. Dig out a sick hill whole, corm and all, and chop it into small pieces so it cannot spread.

items.title: Month 6: Hill up and clean the mats
items.text: Pull soil against the base of each mat with a hoe or spade so it sends up more suckers. Cut off dry leaves and clear the brush between rows.

items.title: Month 8: Second fertilizer
items.text: At about eight months, ring weed first, then spread the fertilizer about 60 to 90 cm away from the plants at the start of the rains, never on dry soil.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Month 20: Cut the mature stalks
items.text: Cut only stalks whose flag leaf, the last small leaf before the flower, has come out. Cut the leaves first with a sickle tied to a bamboo pole, then fell the stalk with a bolo in a slanting cut about 8 cm above the ground so rain does not sit on the stump. Tip: Stalks that already show fruit are past their best and give weaker fiber.

items.title: Month 20: Peel the tuxies the same day
items.text: Slip a thin knife between the outer and middle layers at the base of each leaf sheath and pull off the outer strips (tuxies), two or three fingers wide, keeping the layers from different sheaths apart.

parts.title: Tuxy within a day of felling
parts.text: Pull the felled stalk apart into its leaf sheaths and take off the tuxies the same day, or within 24 hours at most, before the sheaths turn dark and the fiber loses grade.

parts.title: The locnit way
parts.text: With the sheath still on the stalk, slip the thin tuxying knife between the outer and middle layers at the bottom end, grip the loosened strip and pull it off along the whole length, in two or three strips per sheath.

parts.title: The bacnis way
parts.text: Or first peel the whole sheath off the stalk and split it into two or three pieces as wide as you can handle. Make a slanting cut through the inner layer about 2 feet from the butt end, hold it and pull the inner layer away from the tuxy.

parts.title: Keep the layers apart
parts.text: Pile the tuxies by where their sheath sat on the stalk, outer, middle and inner, since each gives a different grade of fiber.

items.title: Month 20: Strip, dry and bundle the fiber
items.text: Pull the tuxies under the stripping knife within a day. Dry the fiber in the sun for a day or in the air for two to three days, keeping it off the ground, then tie it in bundles and store it dry and raised.

parts.title: Strip under the knife
parts.text: Place each tuxy under the stripping knife on its block, press the knife down and pull the tuxy through with a pulling aid. A knife with no teeth gives the cleanest, best paid fiber, and toothed knives give coarser grades. Tip: Keep the knife teeth even by redenting it now and then, or the grade drops.

parts.title: Hang it in thin layers
parts.text: Hang the wet fiber thinly over bamboo poles on sturdy posts, or lay it on a clean cement floor, keeping the tips off the soil. Turn it over after about two hours.

parts.title: Dry it a day, not longer
parts.text: A day of sun, or two to three days of air drying, brings the fiber dry enough to keep, at about 15 percent moisture or less. Drying much longer makes the fiber brittle and weak.
parts.time: 1 day of sun or 2 to 3 days in air

parts.title: Sort by sheath and color
parts.text: Before bundling, sort the dry fiber by the part of the stalk it came from, how clean it is and its color, and never mix grades in one bundle.

parts.title: Tie the bundles
parts.text: Lay two or three twists of abaca fiber side by side on a clean floor, lay the hanks across them and fold them in half until the bundle is the size you can carry, then tie it tight. Use a twist of the same grade as the bundle.

parts.title: Store it dry and raised
parts.text: Keep the bundles on pallets in a cool, dry shed, away from leaves, twigs and trash. Wrap them in plastic bags when hauling them in the rainy season.

items.title: Year 2: Keep cutting every few months
items.text: Come back every 3 to 4 months to cut the next mature stalks from each mat, so none grows too old and weeds have no room.

blocks.text: Watering abaka, stage by stage

Abaca is grown on rain alone, on land with rain spread through the year and soil that drains. Farmers keep the soil damp with shade trees and mulch, and some water young plants once or twice a month in the summer. Rain only on most farms. Young plants in summer are watered by hand with a pail or a hose at the base, in the morning or late afternoon.

blocks.title: Never let abaka go dry at these stages
blocks.text: The first year: young plants need moisture in the summer months.

blocks.caption: Watering schedule for abaka, stage by stage
rows: Plant as the rains begin. If a dry spell follows, water each new hill
A good soaking around the sucker or corm
Once or twice a month in the summer months. No watering in the rains
A good soaking around each hill, then mulch with the cut weeds
No regular watering. Keep the mulch and the shade
No regular watering. Lay the cut leaves and sheaths around the mats

blocks.text:
**Without irrigation.** This is the usual way. Plant at the start of the rains, keep or plant shade trees, and lay cut weeds and leaves around each hill as mulch. Do not plant where the soil stays wet.

**In the dry season.** Water young plants once or twice a month in the summer, and watch older mats for drying leaves. Pseudostem rot and leaf spot also spread in dry weather on stressed plants.

**In the rainy season.** Abaca does not like waterlogged soil. Plant on slopes or land that drains, dig drains where water collects, and never plant in a low, wet spot.

items: **Too little water:** Leaves fold, dry at the edges and break, the new leaves come out slowly, and suckers stop coming.
**Too much water:** Yellow leaves, rotting corms and stalks, and stunted mats in the low spots.

blocks.text: To water better for a higher yield: Keep shade trees and a thick mulch of cut leaves around the mats to hold the soil moisture. Plant only on land with rain spread through the year and good drainage.
Spacing, water and fertilizer for abaka
Spacing

Square planting, usually 2.5 m by 2.5 m (about 1,600 hills a hectare). 2 m by 2 m to 3 m by 3 m depending on the variety, and 1.5 m by 1.5 m (about 4,000 hills) for varieties that make few suckers. In coconut farms many plant in triangles about 2 m apart. Rows run east to west.
Water

Rainfed, on land with rain spread through the year and good drainage. Abaca does not like waterlogged soil. Shade trees and mulch keep the soil damp in the dry months, and some farmers water young plants once or twice a month in summer.
Fertilizer

On the usual small farm, little or none: farmers leave dry leaves, cut weeds and stripping waste to rot around the mats. Where they do put fertilizer, it is ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or complete (14 14 14), a little in the hole at planting, more at about 8 months, and complete fertilizer later on, always spread 60 to 90 cm from the plants after ring weeding. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Ring weeding about half a meter around each hill, strip weeding along the rows, and underbrushing every month or two on a well kept farm, but only now and then on most farms. Hilling up for more suckers, cutting dry leaves, keeping the shade at about half, and digging out hills sick with bunchy top or mosaic.
When and how to harvest

The first stalks are ready at about 16 to 24 months, when the flag leaf appears. After that each mat gives stalks every 3 to 4 months, though many farmers cut only about twice a year. Stalks are topped with a sickle on a pole, felled with a slanting cut, peeled into tuxies the same day, hand stripped with a serrated knife, dried off the ground, bundled with abaca twine and kept dry until sold.
Common mistakes when planting abaka

items: Taking suckers from mats with bunchy top or mosaic, which spreads the virus to the new farm.
Planting abaca next to corn or beans, which carry the aphids that spread virus.
Planting too few hills a hectare and leaving gaps where mats died.
Weeding and cutting only now and then, so stalks grow too old and the fiber is weak.
Leaving stalks or tuxies overnight before stripping, which spoils the fiber color.
Drying fiber on the bare ground where it gets dirty and moldy.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of abaka
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant clean suckers or tissue culture plantlets of a good variety from a trusted nursery.
Fill every missing hill and keep the full number of hills a hectare.
Have the soil tested and fertilize on moist soil after ring weeding.
Check the mats every month and dig out virus sick hills at once.
Harvest every 3 to 4 months, cutting only stalks with the flag leaf out.
Strip within a day, dry the fiber well and store it raised in a dry shed.

blocks.text: Questions about planting abaka

items.a: This guide shows how Filipino abaca farmers in Bicol, Eastern Visayas, Davao, Caraga and other uplands usually set up an abaca farm from suckers or corm pieces and care for it until the first stalks are stripped for fiber. Follow the steps above in order, from getting the field ready to the harvest, then change one thing at a time for a higher yield.

items.q: When do farmers plant abaka in the Philippines?
items.a: Plant as the rains begin so the young plants get steady water. Where rain falls well through the whole year, as on the Pacific side of Bicol, Samar and eastern Mindanao, planting can go on in any month.

items.q: How far apart do you plant abaka?
items.a: Square planting, usually 2.5 m by 2.5 m (about 1,600 hills a hectare). 2 m by 2 m to 3 m by 3 m depending on the variety, and 1.5 m by 1.5 m (about 4,000 hills) for varieties that make few suckers.

items.q: How long before abaka can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 20 months after planting. The first stalks are ready at about 16 to 24 months, when the flag leaf appears.

items.q: How often do you water abaka?
items.a: Planting, planting day to day 30: Plant as the rains begin. If a dry spell follows, water each new hill. Young plants, the first year, day 30 to month 12: Once or twice a month in the summer months. No watering in the rains. Grown mats, month 12 to 20: No regular watering. Keep the mulch and the shade. Water young plants once or twice a month in the summer, and watch older mats for drying leaves.
